passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἵνα μὴ ἐριστικώτερον διαλεγόμενος δαπανῶ τοὺς χρόνους, ἀπαιτῶν δικαίως τῶν ἐμῶν προτάσεών σε τὰς ἀποκρίσεις ποιεῖσθαι, ὡς σοὶ δοκεῖ αὐτὸς ὢν ἐπυθόμην ποιήσομαι τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις. ἐγώ φημι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι τὸν παρεκτικόν, οἷον ὡς αὐτὸν ὁρῶ ποιοῦντα τὸν δημιουργόν, παρέχοντα τὸν ἥλιον ἀγαθοῖς καὶ κακοῖς καὶ τὸν ὑετὸν δικαίοις καὶ ἀδίκοις. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Τοῦτο ἀδικώτατον ὅτι τὰ αὐτὰ δικαίοις καὶ ἀδίκοις παρέχει. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σὺ οὖν ἡμῖν τοῦ λοιποῦ λέγε πῶς ποιῶν ἀγαθὸς ἂν ἦν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Σὲ δεῖ λέγειν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐγὼ λέξω. εἰ μὲν τὰ αὐτὰ παρέχων ἀγαθοῖς καὶ δικαίοις, ἔτι τε κακοῖς καὶ ἀδίκοις, κατὰ σὲ οὐδὲ δίκαιός ἐστιν, καὶ εἰ ἀγαθοῖς ἀγαθὰ παρεῖχεν, κακοῖς τε κακά, δίκαιον ἂν αὐτὸν εὐλόγως ἔλεγες: ποίᾳ οὖν ἔτι πράξει χρώμενος ἂν ἦν, εἰ μὴ ταύτη χρῆται ὁδῷ, κακοῖς μὲν παρέχων τὰ πρόσκαιρα (ἐὰν ἄρα μεταβάλλωνται), ἀγαθοῖς δὲ αἰώνια (ἐάν γε ἐμμείνωσιν); καὶ οὕτως τῷ μὲν πᾶσιν παρέχειν, διαφόροις δὲ χαρίζεσθαι τὸ δίκαιον αὐτοῦ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν καὶ μακρόθυμον ταύτη μᾶλλον, εἰ ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, εὖ πράξασιν δὲ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει. κρίνων δὲ εἰς τέλος καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπονέμων ἑκάστῳ δίκαιός ἐστιν. εἰ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα ὀρθῶς οὕτως ἔχει, ὁμολόγησον· εἰ δὲ οὐ δοκεῖ σοὶ ὀρθῶς ἔχειν, διέλεγξον.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ἅπαξ ἔφην Πᾶς νομοθέτης, εἰς τὸ δίκαιον ἀφορῶν, δίκαιός ἐστιν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἰ ἀγαθοῦ ἐστιν μὴ θεῖναι νόμον, δικαίου δὲ τὸ θέσθαι: καὶ οὕτως ὁ δημιουργὸς ἀγαθός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος· ἀγαθὸς μέν, ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν χρόνων Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωϋσέως ἐγγράφως οὐ φαίνεται τεθεικὼς τὸν νόμον — ἀπὸ δὲ Μωϋσέως εἰς τοὺς δεῦρο χρόνους (ὡς γέγραπται) καὶ δίκαιός ἐστιν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἀπὸ τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου φωνῶν δεῖξον ὅτι τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ἀγαθῷ εἶναι καὶ δικαίῳ. ἐμοὶ γὰρ ἀδύνατον φαίνεται τὸν νομοθέτην ἀγαθὸν ὄντα τὸν αὐτὸν καὶ δίκαιον εἶναι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ὅτι τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτὸ καὶ δίκαιόν ἐστιν, ἐπάκουσον. αὐτὸς ὁ διδάσκαλος ἡμῶν τῷ εἰπόντι Φαρισαίῳ „τί ποιήσας ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσω;“ πρῶτον ἔφη „μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν· ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν, ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς“· εὐθὺς ἐπάξας λέγει „εἰ δὲ θέλεις εἰς τὴν ζωὴν εἰσελθεῖν, τήρησον τὰς ἐντολάς“. τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος „ποίας;“ ἐπὶ τὰς τοῦ νόμου ἔπεμψεν. οὐκ ἂν δὲ ἕτερόν τινα ἀγαθὸν σημαίνων ἐπὶ τὰς τοῦ δικαίου ἀνέπεμπεν ἐντολάς. ὅτι δὲ τὸ δίκαιον ἄλλο ἐστὶν καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἕτερον, καὶ αὐτὸς ὁμολογῶ, ἀλλ’ ὅτι τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐστὶν τὸ ἀγαθῷ εἶναι καὶ δικαίῳ, ἀγνοεῖς. ἀγαθὸς γὰρ ἐστιν μετανοοῦσι μὲν νῦν μακροθυμῶν καὶ ἀποδεχόμενος αὐτούς, δίκαιος δὲ ἐστίν, ὅταν κρίνων τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἑκάστῳ ἀπονέμῃ.

ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖς Οἶδεν ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερος ὑπὲρ αὐτόν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καταλειφθῆναι οὐ δύναται. χάρις οὖν τῷ μὴ εἶναι· τὰ δὲ τῆς γνώμης οἶδεν ἕτοιμα πρὸς ἀγνωμοσύνην. εἰ δὲ εἰδὼς ἀγνώμονά σε ἀποδέχεται, ἐμὲ δὲ εὐγνώμονα ἐπιστάμενος οὐ προσίεται, ἀλόγιστός ἐστι κατὰ τὸν σὸν λόγον, τῷ εὐλόγῳ μὴ κεχρημένος. οὕτω πονηρίας, ὦ Σίμων, ὑπουργὸς ὢν ἀγνοεῖς. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἀπεκρίνατο Πόθεν οὖν τὸ πονηρὸν πέφυκεν, εἰπὲ ἡμῖν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐπειδὴ σήμερον, ἔφη, ἐκβαίνειν ἔφθασας, καὶ ἔφης τοῦ λοιποῦ ὡς βλασφήμου μὴ ἀκούειν ἐμοῦ: αὔριον (εἴγε θέλεις μαθεῖν) ἐλθόντι ὑφηγήσομαι καὶ ὡς θέλεις ἐξετασθῆναί με συγχωρήσω ἄνευ φιλονεικίας. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ὡς ἂν μοι δόξῃ ποιήσω. καὶ τοῦτ᾽ εἰπὼν ἐπορεύθη. τῶν δὲ συνεισελθόντων αὐτῷ οὐδεὶς συνεξῆλθεν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ποσὶν προσπεσόντες Πέτρου ἠξίουν ἐπὶ τῷ συνηρτᾶσθαι τῷ Σίμωνι συγγνώμης τυγχάνειν καὶ ἀποδεχθῆναι μετανοοῦντας. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος προσέμενος αὐτούς τε τοὺς μεταμελομένους καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ὄχλους, ἐπέθηκεν τὰς χεῖρας εὐχάμενος καὶ ἰώμενος αὐτῶν τοὺς πάσχοντας, καὶ οὕτως ἀπολύων παρήγγελλεν αὐτοῖς περὶ τὸν ὄρθρον ταχύνειν. καὶ τοῦτ᾽ εἰπὼν καὶ εἰσελθὼν μετὰ τῶν συνήθων τὰ εἰωθότα πρὸς τὴν ἐπείγουσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐποίησεν, καταλαβούσης ἑσπέρας.

μετὰ τούτων ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ ....... ἐν ὅσῳ ὡς Σίμων φαίνῃ, δημοσίᾳ κήρυξον τὴν σεαυτοῦ μετα ........ Ἐγὼ Σίμων ταῦτα ὑμῖν κηρύσσω. ὁμολογῶ ἀδίκως καταψεύ ........ ἔστι πλάνος, οὐ μιαιφόνος, οὐ γόης οὐδὲ ὅσα ποτὲ φαῦλα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων ἔφθανον ὑπὸ θυμοῦ ἐλαυνόμενος. „δέομαι ὑμῶν“ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ὁ τοῦ πρὸς ὑμᾶς μίσους αἴτιος αὐτῷ γεγονώς, παύσασθε μισοῦντες αὐτόν· τοῦ γὰρ ὑπὸ θεοῦ πρὸς σωτηρίαν κόσμου ἀπεσταλμένου ἀληθοῦς προφήτου ἀληθής ἐστιν ἀπόστολος. διὸ καὶ αὐτὸς συμβουλεύω αὐτῷ ὑμᾶς πείθεσθαι περὶ ὧν κηρύσσει, ἐπεὶ πᾶσα ὑμῶν ἡ πόλις ἄρδην ἀπολεῖται. δι’ ἣν δὲ αἰτίαν ὑμῖν ταῦτα ὡμολόγησα, εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς θέλω. ταύτης τῆς νυκτὸς ἄγγελοί με τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν ἀσεβῆ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὄντα τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας κήρυκι δεινῶς ἐμαστίγουν. „παρακαλῶ οὖν“, μηδ’ ἂν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἄλλοτε ἐπελθὼν κατὰ Πέτρου ἐπιχειρῶν λέγω, μὴ ἀποδέξησθέ με. ἐξομολογοῦμαι γὰρ ὑμῖν Ἐγὼ μάγος, ἐγὼ πλάνος, ἐγὼ γόης. ἔξεστι γὰρ ἴσως μετανοίᾳ ἀπολῦσαι τὰ προπεπραγμένα μοι ἁμαρτήματα.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | repent / repentance where context supports moral-spiritual change | change of mind, reconsider, regret and other contextual renderings | See "Repentance terminology (2026-10-13)"; explain the meaning without homogenizing distinct source expressions |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Repentance terminology (2026-10-13)

The contextual reassessment supersedes the October 11 reorientation default.
Use **repent / repentance** for the moral-spiritual response where the passage
supports it. Familiarity alone is not evidence of accuracy; explain the intended
change of disposition and conduct rather than reducing repentance to sadness
or a change of opinion. Reorientation can explain the concept but is not a
mandatory replacement in reader text. No claim about measured reader reception
or independent scholarly approval is made.

**Context still controls.** Retain regret, remorse, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where those fit the source and local direction.
Preserve contested readings in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17, the alternate turning
reading in Jeremiah 31:19, and distinct turn/return verbs in Acts 3:19 and 26:20.
Use "repentance toward God" in Acts 20:21 because the sentence explicitly gives
that direction; do not insert it into every occurrence of metanoia.

Keep sorrow and repentance distinct in 2 Corinthians 7:9-10. Retain the
relationship between repentance and its fruits, rather than equating the two.
Use "I repent" in Luke 17:4 without requiring proof of completed reform before
forgiveness. Preserve baptismal grammar without deciding symbolic versus causal
interpretations by a vocabulary substitution.

Do not add intensifiers. Keep source-backed emphasis such as the existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" in Hermas 21:4. Keep the corrected
"more joy ... than" in Luke 15:7. Extra-canonical writers retain their own
conceptual frameworks, including adverse changes of mind; do not harmonize
them to a canonical Godward formula. Historical English witnesses and source
transcriptions remain untouched; reader adaptations retain their disclosure.

All **397** previously changed records have an explicit new decision, including
retained exceptions and the four October 12 follow-up records. Earlier wording,
notes, plans, and review history are preserved rather than erased. See the
[full decision ledger](docs/REPENTANCE_REASSESSMENT_2026-10-13.md) and exact,
hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/repentance-contextual-2026-10-13.json`.
These remain editorial drafts, not independent scholarly certifications.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Peter said, “So that I do not spend time in a more contentious debate, rightly demanding that you answer my questions, I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked. I say that the good person is the one who provides, as I see the maker himself doing when he provides the sun to good and evil people and rain to the righteous and unrighteous.” Simon said, “This is most unjust: he provides the same things to the righteous and unrighteous.” Peter said, “Then you tell us from now on how he would act to be good.” Simon said, “You must say.” Peter said, “I will. If, by providing the same things to the good and righteous and also to the evil and unrighteous, he is according to you not even just, and if, by providing good things to the good and bad things to the bad, you would reasonably call him just, what further course of action could he take, if not this way: providing temporary things to the evil, in case they change, and eternal things to the good, provided they remain? Thus, in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients, his justice is good and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who repent and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well. But in judging at the end and assigning to each what is deserved, he is just. If, then, these matters rightly stand this way, acknowledge it; but if they do not seem right to you, refute them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who provides
lexical_decisions.rationale: Goodness is defined through giving/provision in this argument; generous is an alternative, but provision is kept explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he forgives the sins of sinners who repent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The complete μετανοοῦσιν denotes the sinners’ moral-spiritual response in this forgiveness context. “Who repent” follows the October 13 contextual policy, superseding the former mandatory reorientation gloss. It expresses a changed disposition toward wrongdoing, not merely sadness or a new opinion, without requiring proof of already completed reform or supplying an unprinted Godward phrase. The participle is distinct from the encompassing if, which remains separately retained for printed εἰ; forgiveness is not removed or made unconditional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: promises eternal life
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπογράφω can pledge, prescribe, or outline. Promises fits the positive undertaking to those who act well, without claiming automatic possession already.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς σοὶ δοκεῖ αὐτὸς ὢν ἐπυθόμην ποιήσομαι τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied construction juxtaposes participial ὢν with finite ἐπυθόμην irregularly. The English reads this contextually as Peter answering despite having himself asked. A relative ὃς in place of printed ὢν would support a smoother clause but would be conjectural; it is not substituted. The supplied stop between article and noun in τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις is a print punctuation feature, not an alleged OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μὲν πᾶσιν παρέχειν, διαφόροις δὲ χαρίζεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφόροις is taken as a dative of recipients, contrasting everyone with differentiated beneficiaries. It can also mean distinguished or worthy recipients; the main text leaves the difference unspecified. The previous different-gifts rendering would require an instrumental interpretation, by differing gifts, rather than an accusative object; that is a material alternative but the recipient reading is more direct with χαρίζεσθαι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ μακρόθυμον ταύτη μᾶλλον, εἰ ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, εὖ πράξασιν δὲ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who repent and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well.
lexical_decisions.rationale: If preserves εἰ governing the argument through both forgiveness and the promise of life. The participle “who repent” is distinct from that condition; the sentence is not changed into an unconditional assertion by a colon. The contextual repentance gloss does not change the participants or the relation among response, forgiveness, and eternal life.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in case they change
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεταβάλλω is a distinct change expression, not μετανοέω. The moral context permits a change of conduct, but the existing “change” is retained instead of homogenizing this distinct verb into “repent” or adding a Godward formula.

passages.text: Simon said, “I have said it once: every lawgiver, looking toward what is just, is just.” Peter said, “If it belongs to goodness not to lay down a law, and to justice to lay one down, even in this way the maker is both good and just: good because, from Adam’s time until Moses, he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing; and from Moses down to the present times, as it is written, he is also just.” Simon said, “Show from your teacher’s statements that it belongs to the same one to be good and just. For it seems impossible to me that the lawgiver, being good, is himself also just.” Peter said, “Listen to how the good itself is also just. Our teacher himself, when the Pharisee said, ‘What must I do to inherit eternal life?’ first said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ Immediately afterward he added, ‘But if you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.’ When the man said, ‘Which ones?’ he directed him to those of the law. Had he been indicating someone else as good, he would not have referred him to the commandments of the just one. I myself also acknowledge that what is just is one thing and what is good another; but you do not know that being good and just belong to the same one. For he is good in being patient now with those who repent and receiving them; and he is just when, in judging, he assigns to each what is deserved.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγγράφως οὐ φαίνεται τεθεικὼς τὸν νόμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the in-writing qualification and appears, not an absolute claim that there was no divine instruction before Moses.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Pharisee
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s identification of the questioner rather than harmonizing it to a different designation in a familiar Gospel account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who repent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The complete participle concerns the people whom God patiently receives, not a change in God himself. The context supports the moral-spiritual response, so “those who repent” follows the October 13 contextual policy. This is not reduced to regret alone, and no unprinted intensifier or “toward God” phrase is inserted.

passages.text: But you will say, “He knows that no one else is above him, and for this reason he cannot be abandoned.” Then thanks are due to there being no other! Yet he knows the disposition of your mind to be ready for ingratitude. If, knowing you to be ungrateful, he receives you, but knowing me to be grateful does not admit me, according to your account he is irrational, not acting reasonably. Thus, Simon, you are a subordinate of evil without knowing it.” Simon replied, “Then tell us: from where has evil grown?” Peter said, “Since today you already moved to go out and said that from now on you would not listen to me as a blasphemer, if you wish to learn, come tomorrow and I will explain. I will also allow you to examine me as you wish, without contentiousness.” Simon said, “I will do as seems good to me.” After saying this, he went away. None of those who had entered with him went out with him; instead, falling at Peter’s feet, they asked to obtain forgiveness for having been attached to Simon and to be received as they repented. Peter welcomed both those feeling regret and the other crowds, laid his hands on them, praying and healing the afflicted among them. Thus, as he dismissed them, he instructed them to hurry at dawn. After saying this, he went inside with his companions and did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them, since evening had arrived.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Then thanks are due to there being no other
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the ironic thanks and the existential absence, not a moral endorsement of Simon’s fidelity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be received as they repented
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετανοοῦντας describes a moral-spiritual response in the request for forgiveness after association with Simon, so “as they repented” follows the October 13 contextual policy. Their repentance accompanies the request for reception; the translation adds neither a completed-reform requirement nor an unprinted Godward destination.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those feeling regret
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps μεταμέλομαι’s regret or remorse sense distinct from the preceding μετανοέω, rendered repent in its moral-spiritual context. The two surviving source expressions are not homogenized as repentance simply because they describe the same people.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἰωθότα πρὸς τὴν ἐπείγουσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The customary practices are not enumerated here; neither a meal nor a particular prayer is invented.

passages.text: “With these people, in Antioch ....... while you appear as Simon, publicly proclaim your own meta........: ‘I, Simon, proclaim these things to you. I confess: unjustly I katapseu........ is a deceiver, not a murderer, not a sorcerer, nor is he any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him while driven by anger. I beg you—I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you—stop hating him. For he is a true apostle of the true prophet sent by God for the salvation of the world. Therefore I myself also advise you to obey him concerning what he proclaims, since your entire city will be utterly destroyed. I want you to know the reason why I have confessed these things to you. This very night, angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man, as an enemy of the herald of truth. Therefore I appeal to you: even if I myself should come on another occasion and speak while making an attempt against Peter, do not accept me. For I confess openly to you: I am a magician, I am a deceiver, I am a sorcerer. For perhaps it is possible through repentance to put away the sins previously committed by me.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: while you appear as Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν ὅσῳ gives the period during which Faustus visibly bears Simon’s form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not a murderer
lexical_decisions.rationale: μιαιφόνος evokes bloodshed and blood-pollution and functions here as an accusation of murderous violence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅσα ποτὲ φαῦλα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων ἔφθανον
lexical_decisions.chosen: any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: φθάνω with the participle can convey previously or anticipatorily doing something, or going so far as to do it. “Previously hastened to say” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ὁ τοῦ πρὸς ὑμᾶς μίσους αἴτιος αὐτῷ γεγονώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context favors taking πρὸς ὑμᾶς as locating the hatred among or in relation to the listeners and αὐτῷ as marking Peter as the affected person. A more directional reading, “the hatred toward you,” is grammatically possible, but its relationship to αὐτῷ would remain uncertain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄγγελοί με τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν ἀσεβῆ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὄντα τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας κήρυκι δεινῶς ἐμαστίγουν
lexical_decisions.chosen: angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the appositional accusation τὸν ἀσεβῆ and the continuing force of the imperfect verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through repentance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The complete noun μετανοίᾳ appears in a confession of wrongdoing and the prospect of putting away previously committed sins. That context supports “repentance” under the October 13 contextual policy, a moral-spiritual change rather than mere sadness or a new opinion. No destination or intensifier is inserted, and the speculative “perhaps it is possible” remains intact. This complete noun does not license restoring the earlier incomplete μετα........ fragment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to put away the sins previously committed by me
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπολύω can mean release, dismiss, or put away. The construction permits a nuance of either removing the sins or obtaining release from them.

source_issues.source_quote: μετὰ τούτων ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ ....... ἐν ὅσῳ
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints seven dots after Ἀντιοχείᾳ. The unavailable predicate or connective has not been restored, and the translation retains exactly seven dots.

Only the incomplete fragment μετα survives before the eight printed dots. Its identity, completion, and meaning are unavailable. The main text retains “meta” followed by exactly eight dots, not a restored “repentance,” “change,” “reorientation,” or another completed noun. The later complete μετανοίᾳ is translated independently by context; neither the updated terminology policy nor that later noun recovers the lost completion here.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁμολογῶ ἀδίκως καταψεύ ........ ἔστι πλάνος, οὐ μιαιφόνος, οὐ γόης
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints eight dots after the incomplete verbal form καταψεύ. Its completion, object, and any further words are unavailable, so the fragment is transliterated and the gap remains explicit. The surviving clause is ἔστι πλάνος, without a printed negation; the translation therefore preserves “is a deceiver.” Any qualification or negation that might once have stood in the gap has not been restored.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω

The contextual reassessment supersedes the October 11 reorientation default.
Use **repent / repentance** for the moral-spiritual response where the passage
supports it. Familiarity alone is not evidence of accuracy; explain the intended
change of disposition and conduct rather than reducing repentance to sadness
or a change of opinion. Reorientation can explain the concept but is not a
mandatory replacement in reader text. No claim about measured reader reception
or independent scholarly approval is made.

**Context still controls.** Retain regret, remorse, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where those fit the source and local direction.
Preserve contested readings in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17, the alternate turning
reading in Jeremiah 31:19, and distinct turn/return verbs in Acts 3:19 and 26:20.
Use "repentance toward God" in Acts 20:21 because the sentence explicitly gives
that direction; do not insert it into every occurrence of metanoia.

Keep sorrow and repentance distinct in 2 Corinthians 7:9-10. Retain the
relationship between repentance and its fruits, rather than equating the two.
Use "I repent" in Luke 17:4 without requiring proof of completed reform before
forgiveness. Preserve baptismal grammar without deciding symbolic versus causal
interpretations by a vocabulary substitution.

Do not add intensifiers. Keep source-backed emphasis such as the existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" in Hermas 21:4. Keep the corrected
"more joy ... than" in Luke 15:7. Extra-canonical writers retain their own
conceptual frameworks, including adverse changes of mind; do not harmonize
them to a canonical Godward formula. Historical English witnesses and source
transcriptions remain untouched; reader adaptations retain their disclosure.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
